moves.spoken: The standard way to meet the bishop out to c4 is e6, blunting its diagonal — but develop the knight first, keeping the move order flexible before committing the pawn.
The knight comes to f6, and this is actually the most accurate move — it hits the centre and sets up a tactical resource that's about to appear.

Here's the cool device — the centre-fork trick: capture on e4, and the follow-up of grabbing the bishop and striking with d5 tears down the opponent's grip on the centre. A theme that recurs across many openings.

The point of the trick, in full: the central push to d5 both wipes out the opponent's control of the middle and rounds up their important light-squared bishop — emerging a clean pawn up with the centre in hand.
Now just develop conventionally — start by unpinning with the bishop to d7, untangling before pressing the extra material.
Should the knight be taken? Yes — and don't assume no just because the question is posed. The capture improves the pawn structure, and trades are good when you're the one who's ahead.

Bring out the other bishop even though it looks passive — up a pawn with a huge centre, that's fine. Not every piece has to be conquering the frontier at every moment; solid and ahead beats flashy and even.

Draw the sting from the centre with a capture on d4 — and take care not to open the e-file before castling. The reason this recapture is best over the others: at the end of the trade sequence a bishop swings to f6, skewering the queen against the rook and winning the exchange.
